query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐Nb–Ta–based high-entropy superconductors, local lattice distortions arising from atomic size mismatches are the primary factor governing the superconducting properties by tuning the electron–phonon coupling and Fermi level density of states.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloy solid solution (with at least five elements each ≥5 at.%) based on a titanium-rich, heavy transition metal system that is not Nb–Ta dominant.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the alloy by substituting one constituent element with another of a similar electronic character but a measurably different atomic radius to vary the degree of local lattice distortion while keeping the electron count nearly constant.
generation.conditions: All samples are synthesized under identical processing conditions (e.g., controlled melting or powder metallurgy) to ensure single-phase solid solutions, and measured at low temperatures (below 10 K) to clearly resolve superconducting transitions.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local lattice distortion (evidenced by variations in lattice parameters and short-range chemical order) that modulates the microscopic electronic environment.
generation.mechanism: Atomic size mismatch induces local lattice strain, which in turn alters the electron–phonon coupling strength and the density of states at the Fermi level. Moderate lattice distortion can enhance pairing interactions (raising Tc and upper critical field), whereas excessive distortion may disrupt the coherence of the superconducting state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a moderate increase in atomic size mismatch (relative to the baseline) are expected to exhibit an increased superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and higher upper critical field (Hc2) compared to the unmodified alloy. If the lattice distortion becomes too large, superconductivity may be suppressed.
generation.baseline: The starting titanium-rich heavy transition metal HEA with minimal atomic size mismatch and a well-characterized Tc and Hc2.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to bulk, single-phase solid solution HEAs in which the mixing enthalpy and processing conditions prevent the formation of intermetallic precipitates or phase separation, and within the low-temperature superconducting regime (Tc < 10 K).
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the extent of lattice distortion and the superconducting properties is not precisely determined, and the influence of any emerging short-range chemical order remains to be fully isolated from random disorder effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of titanium-rich HEAs where one element is gradually replaced by another element with a different atomic radius but similar valence (to maintain nearly constant electron count). Synthesize all samples under identical conditions to ensure single-phase, disordered structures. Measure their superconducting transition temperatures and upper critical fields using resistivity and magnetic susceptibility techniques.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (to quantify lattice parameter distributions and monitor lattice distortion)
Transmission electron microscopy (for local order analysis)
Resistivity measurements (to determine onset and completion of superconducting transition)
Magnetization measurements (to determine upper critical fields Hc2)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variations in atomic size mismatch (and thus expected lattice distortion) do not correlate with any systematic change in Tc or Hc2, or if increased lattice distortion unexpectedly leads only to a suppression of superconductivity without any initial enhancement, then the hypothesis that local lattice distortions govern superconductivity in these HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa. This is an observation of the zero-resistance state of a superconductor all the way from 1-bar pressure to the pressure of the earth’s outer core without structure phase transition, making the superconducting HEA a promising candidate for new application under extreme condition.Keywords: superconductivity, high pressure, high-entropy alloy AbstractWe report the observation of extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity in the pressurized (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 high-entropy alloy––a material with a body-centered-cubic crystal structure made from five randomly distributed transition-metal elements. It has long been recognized that a critical amount of disorder can suppress superconductivity near the Anderson quantum phase transition. The observed Tc reduction concomitant with a mixing entropy ΔS enhancement in superconducting HEAs seems to agree with that picture. On the other hand, recent analyses of competing interaction-channels in strongly disordered metals predict a Tc enhancement within the BCS framework, when the electron system is tuned to a quantum critical point,. This hypothesis finds support in a recent study of HEA (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x thin films; while each of the binary alloys TaNb and HfZrTi does not show a superconducting transition at or above 2 K, all solid solutions of (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x at various mixing ratios x are superconducting at Tc≤6.9 K. This ’cocktail’ effect suggests an intricate relation between the presence of strong compositional disorder, realized through the random arrangement of five atomic species on a bcc lattice, and superconductivity, which is an interesting question to address experimentally.
